I’ve written the full series: 12 posts that run from the first huts on the Palatine to the fall of Trebizond in 1461. Each is roughly 2,000–2,900 words.

#	Title	Years
1	Wolves, Kings, and a World in Motion	c. 1000–509 BC
2	The Republic Fights for Italy	509–264 BC
3	Carthage, Hannibal, and the Mediterranean	264–146 BC
4	Bread, Blood, and Reform: The Republic Cracks	146–78 BC
5	Strongmen: From Spartacus to Actium	78–27 BC
6	The Augustan Peace and the Julio-Claudians	27 BC–AD 68
7	From the Year of Four Emperors to Marcus Aurelius	AD 69–180
8	Gold to Rust: Commodus and the Crisis of the Third Century	AD 180–284
9	Tetrarchs, Constantine, and the Christian Empire	AD 284–395
10	The Fall of the West	AD 395–480
11	The Eastern Empire Fights Back	AD 476–1025
12	The Long Goodbye: Manzikert to the Fall of Constantinople	AD 1025–1461
How each post is laid out:

Top of the file: a plain-text Title: line and Summary: line, then a --- line. The Markdown body starts after that line.
Rome’s own story: timeline tables for Rome’s wars and conquests, with mutinies, revolts and usurpers given their own rows or sections.
“Meanwhile, around the world” table: each row is a date, a place, what happened, and what Rome was doing at that moment.
“Things you might not have known happened at the same time”: short highlights such as Zama and the founding of the Han dynasty both in 202 BC, Teutoburg and Wang Mang’s seizure of China’s throne both in AD 9, and Constantinople falling seven weeks before the last battle of the Hundred Years’ War.
“Sources and notes”: the ancient writers, modern books and Wikipedia links I drew on, plus a “Flags” paragraph naming dates that are traditional, disputed or likely legend.
Before you publish:

Check the links. I didn’t look anything up online; it’s all from my own knowledge. I also didn’t open the links to check they work, so please click through them once.
Formatting: I wrote to your blog’s own Markdown rules: tables in GitHub style, a blank line after each table, no nested lists, one-line blockquotes only and no raw HTML. A script confirmed every table has matching column counts and ends with a blank line.
